name: LTE cells
label: LTE
notes: LTE base stations (E-UTRA downlink), decoded by OnAir's receiver through the onair-rx handler; the row has no decoder of its own, so only a handler runs it. It reads what each cell broadcasts, not traffic: the cell search, the MIB and the system information. Each event is a cell, first when it is found and again when a member changes: `freq_hz` (the raster frequency: the nearest channel of TS 36.101's table, else the 100 kHz grid), `pci` (the physical cell id; a cell whose MIB is not read yet has `freq_hz` and `pci` only), `bandwidth_hz` (the MIB's), `mcc`, `mnc` (numbers), `tac` and `cell_id` (once SIB1 is read), `sibs` (the SIB numbers decoded so far) and `snr_db`. Nothing is decrypted. The handler takes 20 MHz of IQ, OnAir's usual: it holds a carrier of any width whole, so the system information of a 20 MHz cell is read as well as a 5 MHz one's (a 5 MHz cell needs 4.6 MHz of input at the least), and a job on a narrower band is resampled up to it. Each system information message goes to a packet capture as GSMTAP (type 13, LTE RRC) in IPv4 and UDP to port 4729 (link type 101). Ranges and bands: the spans are downlinks of E-UTRA operating bands in 3GPP TS 36.101 (Table 5.5-1), across regions, neighbouring bands merged: 460 to 470 MHz (bands 31, 72 and 73), 617 to 652 MHz (71), 728 to 821 MHz (12, 13, 14, 17, 20 and 28), 852 to 894 MHz (5, 18, 19, 26 and 27), 925 to 960 MHz (8), 1452 to 1559 MHz (11, 21, 24 and 32), 1805 to 1995 MHz (2, 3, 25, 33, 35, 36, 37 and 39), 2010 to 2025 MHz (34), 2110 to 2200 MHz (1, 4, 10, 23, 65 and 66), 2300 to 2400 MHz (30 and 40), 2496 to 2690 MHz (7, 38 and 41) and 3400 to 3800 MHz (22, 42, 43 and 48). The table has other bands these spans leave out (29, 52 and 53 among them): identify does not try the row there, and a job started by hand runs there as anywhere. Carriers are 1.4 to 20 MHz wide. **The entry runs onair-rx with `--drop`, so a replay can miss**: OnAir's LTE search takes about 2.8 s for each 0.2 s of input at 20 MHz on the build host (0.8 s at 4.6 MHz), so without `--drop` the job would fall behind real time; with it the receiver decodes the blocks it has time for (about one in fourteen) and reads a cell that stays on the air within a few blocks. `capture_decode` replays paced in real time, in blocks of 50 ms: measured on the build host, a replay of the row's generated 20 MHz capture (0.9 s, and 7.2 s of it looped) gave one event, the cell whole (MCC, MNC, TAC, cell identity, SIBs 1 to 5), with no input dropped by the wrapper. A short replay is read from its first 0.2 s block, since the blocks that come while it is decoded are skipped; a feed faster than real time loses most of its input under `--drop`. Listing bar: measured on the build host (12 cores) through a scratch node's release build, 30 s of the generated capture looping on a file source and fed in real time; the job skipped no input, onair-rx used 1.08 of a core and the node 0.45 of a core (load average 4.8 to 4.2). Measured on OnAir's 5 MHz cell and on its 20 MHz cell (1.08 of a core each, load 4.1 to 4.2), both input at 20 MHz, with `--drop` (without it the receiver cannot keep real time here).
